Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Piedmont: The rainfall caused one of the most severe flood events in recent history in Piedmont. It rained heavily and persistently in all the major Alpine valleys of Piedmont, from the Susa Valley through the Aosta Valley, the Lanzo Valley, and the Canavese to the Sesia Valley and the Eschen Valley, resulting in widespread flooding throughout the Po Basin. In addition to immense property damage, there were 23 fatalities, 128 injuries, 11 missing persons, and around 40 homeless individuals. In the upper reaches of the Po, the Pellice Valley was particularly affected by the flooding; in Moncalieri and Turin, city districts near the Po were flooded, with the river at Turin temporarily carrying 2,300 cubic meters of water per second, significantly exceeding the severe flood of 1994. It was the largest flood in Turin since 1839. During the flood, bridges over the Orco collapsed at Noasca and Bardonetto, the bridge over the Stura at Robassomero, a railway bridge at Ivrea (Settimo Vittone), and additional road bridges in the Canavese were destroyed by the water. In the Po plain below Turin, the side dikes of the Po broke in several places, and numerous towns were flooded; the flood zone extended downstream to an area in Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna.

Canton of Ticino: The water level of Lake Maggiore reached its highest level since 1867. On October 14, the lake overflowed its banks and slowly flooded the old town of Locarno. By October 17, the water kept rising and eventually reached a record level that had not been measured in the 20th century. The flooding of Lake Maggiore affected not only Locarno in Ticino but also residential and commercial areas, sports facilities, public buildings, wastewater treatment plants, and clinics in the municipalities of Ascona, Brissago, Gordola, Minusio, Muralto, Tenero-Contra, and Gambarogno. It was only on October 25 that the water had flowed from Sesto Calende into the Ticino River towards the Po, allowing the lake to retreat back into its normal basin.

Canton of Valais: In the canton of Valais, the event affected the entire Rhone catchment area above Lake Geneva. On October 14 and 15, numerous streams and rivers overflowed their banks, large areas were flooded, and debris flows destroyed numerous houses, buried villages and transport infrastructure. Near Stalden-Neubrück, a debris flow destroyed five buildings and disrupted the cantonal road and the Brig-Visp-Zermatt railway line; the Vispa, dammed by the debris flow, flooded the Stalden wastewater treatment plant. Below Zermatt, a lake formed due to a debris flow, submerging several buildings. The BVZ railway line between Brig and Zermatt was interrupted, being reopened only after 24 days. Debris flows destroyed houses in Mörel, the Binntal, Naters, and Baltschieder, with the Baltschiederbach flooding a settlement area. Between Brig-Glis and Visp, the Gamsa flowed onto the construction site of the A9 motorway and over railway lines. As a secondary consequence, severe flooding occurred in Lower Valais, with the Vissingen Canal overflowing in Sion and near Chamoson the Rhone levee breaching, exposing critical infrastructure. In total, 1,027 hectares in the Rhone plain were eventually flooded.

Gondo: The most severe single disaster affected the village of Gondo. A landslide above the village caused a protective wall to collapse on October 14, and the mass of rock, earth, and debris hit several buildings below and slid further down into the Doveria gorge, which was experiencing flooding. Ten houses were destroyed, and 13 people lost their lives. The three-hundred-year-old Stockalper Tower was damaged. Along the Doveria and the Grosses Wasser river in the Zwischbergen Valley, flooding also destroyed protective structures and riverbank reinforcements.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Num: 129 houses, a synagogue, and the Bykhov market
Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Disaster: On April 10, 1942, repair workers reached the remains of the pipe where Soviet soldiers had planted explosives. When the embankment broke in the second half of the day, the wave instantly swept away all the repair workers. Within 20 minutes, most people, 129 houses, a synagogue, and the Bykhov market were swept into the Dnieper. Unconscious bodies gathered on the banks were placed in one pit. Most of the deceased were not buried due to the swampy deposits of silt and clay, which prevented access to the river for several weeks. Bodies in the dried silt were still being found throughout the year.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Affected areas in Herford: The article states 'The areas particularly affected were the Neustadt, the settlement area at the upper Werre course, part of the old town, the Radewig, as well as the densely populated lower course of the Werre. In the streets of the city center, the water was up to 1.50 meters high in some places. The wells and pumping stations for drinking water supply were also endangered by the flooding. Fatally, the flood wave of the Aa – usually occurring four to six hours earlier than that of the Werre – coincided with it. The masses of water also tore away the Hansa Bridge, which stood just behind the confluence of the Aa into the Werre, interrupting the route of the Herford narrow-gauge railway until May 1949.'

Adjacent areas: The article explains that 'Above and below Herford, other places were affected by the floodwaters. Upstream in Bad Salzuflen, the Werre and in Lemgo, the Bega overflowed their banks and flooded almost the entire Neustadt. ... Downstream in Löhne, parts of the river-adjacent districts of Löhne-Ort, Gohfeld, Mennighüffen, and Obernbeck were flooded, with Obernbeck being the most affected. In Bad Oeynhausen, where the Werre flows into the Weser, parts of Dehme and Rehme were submerged in the floods. ... In the Sielpark, ... the area was underwater. The Werste fire department was on duty day and night, supplying the affected population with essentials using inflatable boats. There were also floods along the Weser in Minden.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Header 'Altare and Val Bormida': 'No victims, but millions and millions of old lire in damages. The Val Bormida was also hit hard, especially Altare and Ferrania suffered significant damage. The glass city was devastated by that event, with the historic center invaded by mud, streets turned into torrents, cars piled up by the fury of the water, shops and basements completely flooded, as seen in the images archived by the then broadcaster TeleValBormida. The railway station was closed, connections interrupted and ensured only by the Savona-Turin highway. In Cadibona (Quiliano), a house remained balanced on the hill for years. The flood also hit the Cairnese district, and the Ferrania plant was evacuated in the early afternoon. In Altare, which was left without electricity for hours, it took years to restore the situation, and one of the most significant interventions at the end of the last millennium was the construction of a diversion channel on Via Gramsci to manage underground waters. A true catastrophe, albeit without human victims, but one that many still remember as an apocalyptic scenario.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Header 'British Hong Kong': The text states, 'The typhoon passed 95 kilometers (60 nautical miles) south of Hong Kong, causing certain damages. Many houses in the Kowloon area collapsed, including over 130 houses in Cheung Sha Wan, and all the squatter huts in Kowloon Tong were blown away. A bus overturned on Salisbury Road. Additionally, 2 ocean‐going vessels and 9 fishing boats were damaged. The storm resulted in 15 deaths and 22 injuries.'

Header 'Portuguese Macau': The content notes, 'In Joaquim Baião Simões' book "Macau and the Typhoons" (1985), it records the typhoon on August 20, 1927, which caused loss of life and immeasurable damage in Macau. The cruiser "Democrata," anchored in the Inner Harbor, nearly sank, and the Governor's Palace was also damaged. The Chinese‐language newspaper reported four drowning deaths. After the storm, the South Bay coastline was in complete disarray, with wreckage from numerous fishing boats washed up along the embankment. In the area of Sá Lei Tau, a shipyard was blown down. On Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro and near the Army Club, large trees were uprooted.'

It mentions storm surges in the harbor (sea level rising to 3.2 m and a 4.57 m storm surge in Tai Po), damage to naval infrastructure (HMS L9 swept out of the naval dockyard, dockyard outer wall destroyed), a steamship being swept from Kowloon Bay to Yau Ma Tei pier and sank, 20 ships being washed ashore along the coastline from Shau Kei Wan to Stonecutters Island, 90% of ships at Taikoo Dockyard sinking, over 300 vessels affected in the Shau Kei Wan typhoon shelter, and further damage at Causeway Bay, Yau Ma Tei, Central Blake Pier, Star Ferry Pier, and Connaught Road. No monetary values are provided.

Portuguese Macau: The article details that on August 18, 1923 the Portuguese Navy hoisted Typhoon Signal No. 11 (lasting 13.5 hours) during which the typhoon caused significant damage. According to Joaquim Baião Simões' book 'Macau and the Typhoons (Macau e os Tufões)', about 200 houses and 24 shipyards were destroyed or damaged and 50 ships were sunk, with the disaster resulting in over 400 deaths and 52 injuries. No explicit economic (monetary) damage figures are provided.

Header: Portuguese Macau – 'Macau experienced strong winds and heavy rain, with the Outer Harbour area being the most threatened. An unmanned boat sank at sea, the New Reclamation swimming area was destroyed, the Nam Van Friendship Stadium was damaged, and many rooftop drying racks and shop signs were blown away. Several small trees on Avenida de Venceslau de Morais were uprooted. A shipyard in the Areia Preta area collapsed, causing significant cargo losses but no casualties. Streets such as Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro, Rua da Felicidade, Rua dos Mercadores, Rua da Praia do Manduco, and the San Kio district were flooded, with water levels exceeding one foot in some areas. Several old houses on Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro collapsed, injuring a police officer.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Netherlands header and newspaper report: 'Utrecht, August 2. Yesterday evening at half past seven, a terrible storm arose here, lasting until half past eight; but the worst occurred within a quarter of an hour: the sky was continuously lit and aflame, and it was terrifying to hear the thunder and dreadful winds, accompanied by the collapse of chimneys, roofs, facades, and towers, which brought an uncommon astonishment to everyone, and caused many to speak of an earthquake: the church of the Dom up to the choir lay with pillars and all underfoot as a heap of rubble by half past seven, without the Dom Tower being damaged in any way [...] In the immediate vicinity of the city of Utrecht, in Vleuten, Jutphaas, Bunnik, Houten, and IJsselstein, church towers collapsed. In other areas of present-day Netherlands, churches collapsed in Asperen, Hellouw, Hippolytushoef, and Den Ilp. On a large scale, houses were destroyed in Hilversum and Landsmeer. In places such as Amsterdam, ships broke loose or sank. There was also significant damage in North Holland up to Texel.'

Netherlands: 'By 7 p.m., the storm front reached the city of Utrecht. The most famous structure in the city damaged by the downbursts was the Dom Church. The nave of this church collapsed. Towers of four other church buildings also collapsed: those of the Sint-Jacobskerk (now Jacobikerk), Sint-Nicolaaskerk (now Nicolaikerk), Buurkerk, Pieterskerk, and Agnietenkerk. Other damaged structures included houses and several windmills. Trees were damaged or blown over, and many people lost their lives due to collapses. Shortly after the disaster, Herman Saftleven was commissioned by the Utrecht city council to create a series of detailed drawings of the devastating downbursts and their consequences. The following report appeared in the Oprechte Haerlemse Saterdaegse Courant: "Utrecht, August 2. Yesterday evening at half past seven, a terrible storm arose here, lasting until half past eight; but the worst occurred within a quarter of an hour: the sky was continuously lit and aflame, and it was terrifying to hear the thunder and dreadful winds, accompanied by the collapse of chimneys, roofs, facades, and towers, which brought an uncommon astonishment to everyone, and caused many to speak of an earthquake: the church of the Dom up to the choir lay with pillars and all underfoot as a heap of rubble by half past seven, without the Dom Tower being damaged in any way [...] In the immediate vicinity of the city of Utrecht, various places were also affected; in Vleuten, Jutphaas, Bunnik, Houten, and IJsselstein, church towers collapsed. In other areas of present-day Netherlands, churches collapsed due to the storm in places such as Asperen, Hellouw, Hippolytushoef, and Den Ilp. On a large scale, houses were destroyed in Hilversum and Landsmeer. In places such as Amsterdam, ships broke loose or sank. There was also significant damage in North Holland up to Texel."

Several coast guard vessels and boats, in collaboration with private boats, transported a significant portion of the population from the wider areas of Polychrono, Hanioti, and Pefkochori to the shores of Sithonia, where they remained until it was confirmed that the fire was no longer a threat to the nearby settlements.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Polychrono, Halkidiki: 'On the afternoon of August 21, there were initial reports of smoke west of the settlement of Polychrono, which prompted an immediate response from the fire department. However, a few hours later, Kassandra was declared in a state of emergency as the fire got out of control and created a unified front several kilometers long, extending to the borders of the settlement of Pefkochori. The settlement of Polychrono was the first to suffer damage to residences located within the forested area, while traffic was halted with the main aim of avoiding congestion on the main road arteries of the region.'

Chanioti, Halkidiki: 'The settlement of Chaniotis received the first evacuation warnings as soon as the fire went out of control and dangerously approached the village's boundaries. Traffic had been interrupted, and any access from Nea Skioni or Polychrono was impossible as a sea evacuation was ordered, leading most residents towards the sea. Several damages were observed within the settlement as it was located right in the middle of the fire, which was burning the forest core of south-central Kassandra, resulting in several small fire outbreaks within residential complexes, hotels, and the central coastal park. The fire reached the settlement's boundaries from the west and north, making the atmosphere suffocating and, in some cases, crossing the national road of N. Potidaia-Paliouri, which serves as a border between the settlement and the former pine forest, causing damage to nearby buildings.'

Pefkochori, Halkidiki: 'The settlement of Pefkochori, along with that of Nea Skioni, suffered the least damage as the fire was extinguished just a few hundred meters from the urban area. However, in the wider area of Pefkochori, houses within the forested area were completely destroyed, including a hotel located in the panorama of the settlement.'

Cold wave of 1956: 'The episode was also very intense in Mallorca, where it is still remembered by those who lived through it as the Year of the Snow. A minimum temperature of -13.5 °C was reached, and snow depths of more than 50 cm were recorded. The agricultural damage was immense, as all the fields remained frozen, and it had significant economic effects.'

The olive trees: 'In the Principality, the olive trees that had been pruned during January suffered greatly when early sap rise met intense and prolonged frosts and strong tramontane winds, causing branch splitting and even complete trunk cracking. Consequently, the damaged olive trees were uprooted, and 62% of the area occupied by olive trees in 16 municipalities of Alt Empordà disappeared in the following years.'

Hurricane of November 19, 1973: 'In the lower reaches of the Hunte, Lesum, and Ochtum, which were not yet secured by barriers at the time, severe damage occurred, including to summer dikes, roads, and areas in front of the main dikes. On the islands in the Lower Weser as well as on Krautsand, buildings located on insufficiently high mounds were flooded for the second time within a week. On the East Frisian Islands and on Sylt, dune erosion occurred. The situation at the sea dike in front of Christianskoog in the Meldorfer Bay also became critical.'

Hurricane of December 6, 1973: 'Although there were no dike breaches, there was very severe damage in the flooded harbor area in Hamburg, where numerous businesses were caught off guard by the unexpectedly high surge. The sea dike in front of Christianskoog, which had not been raised after the 1962 storm surge, was again severely damaged and could only be held with massive deployment of emergency forces.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: From the 'Tochigi Prefecture' header: '219 people were dead or missing, approximately 8,200 houses were completely destroyed or washed away, and 315 millimeters of rainfall were recorded in Ashio. The Watarase River flooded, and the significant damage in Ashio later became the basis for the typhoon's name. In Ashio Town, the Mikonai Elementary School was washed away, among other damages. Additionally, a debris flow occurred in Nikko Chugushi. The sediment that flowed into Lake Chuzenji caused 3-meter-high waves, resulting in casualties at inns and other locations. These waves flowed over Kegon Falls into the Daiya River, washing away the Shinkyo and Otani bridges. The "Narabi Jizo" statues at Kanmangafuchi were also washed away. It is said that the appearance of Urami Falls changed due to this typhoon. Currently, the Registered Tangible Cultural Property "Moka High School Memorial Hall" at Tochigi Prefectural Moka High School is a building reconstructed the following year after the school building was damaged by this typhoon.'

Affected by Kemi, power outages were reported in many areas in southern Taiwan. Taiwan Power Company stated that the heavy rain caused power outages for a total of 13,500 households in Kaohsiung City at one point, with sporadic outages in Pingtung County and Tainan City, which were restored after emergency repairs. Additionally, flooding occurred in areas such as Jiadong Township and Linbian Township in Pingtung County, with traffic control implemented on multiple road sections within the county. Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: Chronology: On the evening of November 18, 2023, a hurricane‐force wind struck Astana. According to meteorologists, the wind speed reached 23 m/s and caused significant damage (building wall cladding was torn off, roofs were ripped off, and advertising banners collapsed).

Chronology: On the evening of the same day and into the night of November 19, squally winds with a force of 30 m/s hit the Pavlodar region bordering Russia, resulting in power outages in about 100 settlements, 42 roofs of residential and administrative buildings torn off, and heating supply disrupted in Pavlodar itself.

Chronology: On the night of November 19, hurricane‐force winds, increasing to 32 m/s, struck the Altai Krai. Due to fallen trees on the roadway, traffic was partially halted on several highways (including the K-03 highway, Ribbon Forest highway in Barnaul, and the Biysk-Sorokino road). In Barnaul and Biysk, the wind felled numerous trees, damaged cars, and destroyed roofs, leaving seventy settlements without electricity. Consequences: In Biysk, the wooden dome of the church in honor of the Kazan Icon of the Mother of God collapsed.

Chronology: On the morning of November 19, hurricane‐force winds, increasing to 35 m/s and above, struck Novokuznetsk. In parts of the city, there was no electricity or water supply, trucks overturned, and fir trees were uprooted.
Chronology: The hurricane raged in Krasnoyarsk and then moved to the Irkutsk region, cutting off electricity in several districts.

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: History: 'At 8:45 PM, a powerful tornado began to form over the Euganean Hills, particularly affecting Teolo and Rovolon in the province of Padua.'
History: 'At 9:05 PM, the tornado caused the partial collapse of the Zen Foundries in Albignasego, resulting in the first death and injuries.'
History: 'Entering the province of Venice, the storm damaged more than 60 houses, with four injuries reported in Vigonovo, Tombelle, Caltana, and Fossò.'

History: 'Upon reaching the San Marco Basin, between the Lido of Venice and Sant'Elena, the tornado struck the 400-ton motor vessel Aquileia (causing one injury) and only partially affected the motor vessel Altino.'

History: 'At 9:36 PM, motorboat 130 of line 2, operated by ACNIL, while docking at Sant'Elena, was fully hit by the tornado, which lifted and submerged the vessel, resulting in 21 deaths among the approximately 50 passengers.'
History: 'The entire island of Sant'Elena was devastated, with uprooted trees (one of which killed a person) and damaged buildings, including the Celli shipyard and the marina.'
History: 'Finally, at 9:42 PM, the tornado struck the Ca' Savio campsite, where it caused 12 deaths and 141 injuries among the 300 people present.'

Other events: 'On the afternoon of June 15, 2007, a powerful tornado struck the 30,000 spectators attending the mega concert of the Heineken Jammin' Festival at San Giuliano Park in Mestre. The wind caused the collapse of the six towers of the sound system, injuring 30 people.'

Specific_Instance_Per_Administrative_Are.Annotation: How does it manifest? - 'What happened in Bellano on Saturday, June 25? Around 2:00 PM, shortly after the start of the first regatta, a storm broke out: the Menaggino, a wind particularly feared by the people of Bellano, formed within a few minutes and strengthened to 50-60 knots, followed by a heavy hailstorm. No vessel was spared; in the end, there was a lot of fear, some damage to sails and hulls, but no serious harm to people, all of whom were rescued.'

The dates on which the Menaggino manifested itself - 'June 25, 2005: It originated from a disturbance with winds of 50-60 knots that hit Ascona at 2:00 PM and Menaggio at 3:00 PM, while the annual Bellanasco Cup was taking place between Bellano and Dervio. 32 capsized catamarans in addition to countless smaller class boats, torn sails, broken shrouds, and boats adrift that later became stranded on the shores of Dervio and Dorio. The recovery of the boats was completed at 8:00 PM.'

Administrative_Areas_Annotation: The header 'Where does it come from?' states that the wind reaches Lake Como (in Italy) via the Val Menaggio, which emerges from Switzerland. Other parts of the text reference Italian locations such as Bellano, Menaggio, and Lake Como.
